docs.title: Hearth
docs.text:
The choice: to use the stove I got for free, or buy a new one. If I use the existing stove, over-large and with a metal box around it, the only real option is to keep it on ground level, and vent hot air upwards.

I like the idea of improvising some kind of a cob-oven type shield enclosure, with sheets of metal, clay, maybe using steel drums.

There could be some kind of insulated box around it, a walk in furnace room, near the center but towards the low end of the house.

Borrowed ladders, borrowed time. Halloween, Kurt. A mobile game where you catch cute animals and make them fight.

Midterms coming up.

A stove. The heart. It wants to beat with a reflection of larger patterns. The meta choice is to do what makes the most sense at the time given the available resources. I wish I had more relational wealth by now.

These are the tracks laid, paths molded, willows of dendrites and electrical storms planted.

Things not said, to be deleted later:

That's kind of a good joke, to have an empty list, meaning there is nothing to be deleted, or that it had been.

The stove heart. Stoned hearth. Is it gifted or taken from a shelf, a box?

Sometimes tinkering, experimental or incremental building isn't the way to go.

The roof needs to go in. Blown Cellulose or Fiberglass Batts Harlequined battes. Bats in the roof.

docs.title: Treehouse Project
docs.text:
A year ago I became the proud but somewhat terrified custodian of the Treehouse at Dancing Rabbit: A one-bedroom off-grid cabin held above the Missouri prairie like a Baba Yaga hut by twelve Osage posts.

It is a beautiful--some would say ridiculous--structure, that the previous proprietor had been renting out as a three-season Bed and Breakfast, despite lacking siding, heating, insulation, or electricity.

My goal is to make it livable, with functional systems, by this winter. Currently, I'm looking for ways to mitigate the summer heat (an 'aluminet' 20x16 heat-shielding shade cloth should be arriving tomorrow to soften the greenhouse effect of the west-facing wall of windows).

This website documents my progress and asks the community for input on various aspects of the project. One of the advantages of living in a cooperative ecovillage, and having smart and ecologically minded friends, is the availability of good advice, and this is my way of asking for it.

docs.title: August 12, 2026 - Switches, Fuses, Wires
docs.text:
The Treehouse has solar.

At the end of last month, my father and brother drove up from Kansas City with green 2x4s, wires, screws, and electric tools. I watched as the work and decisions that would have taken me months happened in one afternoon.

Now I'm here trying to understand what I have on my wall, and figuring out how to install fuses, breakers, bus bars, and switches.

As before, I'm looking for help in knowing what to order, and how to safely wire it all up. Let me know if you have any interest in helping with or watching the physical wiring, and I'll tell you when the parts get here.

docs.title: Story
docs.text:
"You don't think he's on the roof, do you?" my brother asked. We'd taken a break, gone to cool off by the pond. My father had kept working, wanting to get everything installed that day, rather than staying the night. Considering all that had to get done: running wires through the walls, hooking the batteries to the controller, the shunt, and the inverter, I was skeptical we could finish. I also realized the next step would be mounting the panels, and we'd left our father by himself.

"Yeah," I said, "he's probably on the roof."

docs.title: Parts
docs.text: Component Spec Why 200Amp ANL Fuse 200A, includes 12" 1/0 AWG cable, 5/16" stud Protects the shared cable from the battery bank to the inverter, sized to the inverter's real peak draw at full load Disconnect Switch 12V/24V/48V, 300A continuous Single manual off-point for the whole system — so you can work on any downstream wiring without disconnecting live cables Positive and Negative Bus Bars Matched pair, 250A, 5/16" studs Common tie point for every branch circuit instead of stacking wires on the battery terminal directly; negative bar routes through the SmartShunt's system side so it sees all outgoing current Wire Stripper and Crimper Ratcheting mechanism Makes the actual mechanical connection inside a heat-shrink terminal — the crimp is the electrical joint, the heat step after is just a weatherproof seal Crimp Kit Assorted ring/spade/butt terminals, 22-10 AWG, adhesive-lined heat shrink Terminates wire ends onto bus bar studs, fuse block terminals, and switches Multimeter True RMS, auto-ranging, AC/DC Confirming a circuit is actually dead before touching it, checking voltage and continuity while troubleshooting Switches 12V 20A waterproof rocker, LED lit Manual on/off for individual circuits downstream of the fuse block Fuse Box Blue Sea ST Blade Fuse Block, 12 circuit + ground, 100A Houses the individual branch fuses below, gives every DC load its own protected, switchable circuit Fuses ATO blade assortment, 2A-35A Matched to each branch's actual wire gauge and load — a light circuit and a charging circuit don't need the same rating

docs.title: Battery Fuses
docs.text:
One thing they didn't bring, and that I knew was necessary to run the setup safely, were fuses and breakers. The diagrams from user guides I was looking at always showed fuses in between each connection, and the internet suggested that each fuse needed to be matched to the right gauge of wire, and the Amps needed to trigger it.

A few days after his visit, my dad emailed recommending "a 30 amp DC breaker in series on each battery". My method has been to add everything either AI or people have told me I need to an Amazon cart, and then having another LLM review it and tell me what is wrong or missing.

Claude, in a recent iteration, told me "your 2000W inverter at 12V can pull upward of 150-160A under load...the 30A DaierTek breakers are too small for this role; they're right-sized for individual branch circuits (a light, a USB charger, a small accessory), not the main battery feed. You need a single higher-rated fuse or breaker (ANL fuse in the 150-200A range is typical for a 2000W inverter setup) inline at the battery terminal, before anything else."

I'm inclined to believe my father, with a life-time of engineering experience, over newly awakened ghosts of disembodied syntax, but I wanted to hear other opinions, too.

Let me know if you think any of the following things are unnecessary, the wrong type, or if you know of a better way.

docs.title: Disconnect Switch
docs.text: I need a way to manually cut off the power from the batteries to everything else, so I don't shock myself playing with wires.

docs.title: Bus Bars
docs.text: My understanding is that while wiring everything to the battery bolt like we have now is fine, but adding a fuse box or bus bar will be safer, and on the negative end allow me to connect different DC outputs.

docs.title: Heat shrink, crimp kit, ratcheting crimper
docs.text:
This is where I feel like AI might be selling me things I don't need. This is all supposedly to get the wiring crimped onto the bus bars.

I'm pretty sure I've seen wire strippers and crimpers around the ecovillage. Any leads?

In order to heat-crimp wires, a heat gun is recommended, but you can also use a lighter...one place where I'm saving money.

docs.title: Multimeter
docs.text: This seems like a tool worth having, so I know what is going through the wires.

docs.title: Fuse Box
docs.text: I eventually want to have several DC loads (lights, etc) going through a fuse box. My dream is to wire everything through a Raspberry Pico to control it with code, but that can wait for more essential projects.

docs.title: Story, Continued
docs.text:
He was on the roof.

We screwed the frame into the metal, a weird, south-facing angle, close to 45 degrees, using dabs of silicon rubber to stop any leaks.

We'd gone to Rose hardware in Memphis to buy nuts to go with bolts we'd found in the machine shed. My dad had refused to buy washers, because the price (thirty cents or so each) was too much.

When I mis-measured distances between drill holes, and had to wiggle the drill around to get the bolt to fit, I said, "Now the bolt is just going to sink down into the hole..."

"Too bad we don't have any washers," my dad replied.

There was power. They'd brought a couple lights to plug into the inverter, and my dad showed me how to take one of the led strips ("There are the lights I take to Burning Man, but I guess I can buy more") and by touching the right wires together, got them to luminate in different colors.

I left them on, live wires crimped into little plastic caps, wound up in a spool. After they left, I went back up and found that the plastic spool was melting, along with the adhesive on the back of the strip. I untwisted the wires, and unwound the lights, deciding not to try to wire anything else up to DC until I at least had some fuses hooked up.

docs.title: July 16, 2026 - Initial Solar Setup Planning
docs.text:
The problem of choosing an off-grid solar setup for a small, stilt-supported cabin has a particular combination of my own lack of expertise, and significant expense, that makes me nervous enough to sincerely request any input you might have.

Note: the selection of components, as well as the reasoning, is the result of my using Artificial Intelligence (mostly Claude), and not my own understanding. This is one of the reasons I would like humans, whose opinions I value, in the loop.

docs.title: The Gear
docs.text:
Note: Component name links to site where I plan to order from.

Component Spec Why Solar panels 2× Renogy 200W I plan to use solar to run some LED lights, charge a phone and laptop, and run some tools with minor draw like a small fan. 400W should be enough for this, but not anything like a fridge or mini-split. Two panels rather than one gives me more options for placement and replacement. Should pair well with the 100Ah/12V battery. Charge controller 40A MPPT Right size for the panel array, MPPT should get more power than cheaper PWM controllers. The 400W array should only draw roughly 33A max at 12V Battery 100Ah LiFePO4 LiFePO4 will last longer than a lead-acid battery. Also lighter and smaller. Inverter 2000W pure sine Apparently more efficient and safer than modified sine. Battery monitor Victron SmartShunt This should let me monitor the battery's state of charge (the current going in and out). Hooks up with Bluetooth app to analyze data and trends.

docs.title: What I'd like feedback on
docs.text: Mostly I just don't want to do anything stupid, or waste money. Once I have the system, my father has offered to help install it, but the more eyes and hands on this project the better I will feel.

docs.title: How to weigh in
docs.text: Email, call, or talk to me in person! If you don't have time to reach out in the relevant window, or don't feel like you have anything to add on the solar question, don't worry: there will be plenty of other opportunities to offer advice or criticism in the future.

It's writing group night, and I'm in the mercantile, wondering if I remember how to upload changes to a webpage.

I almost didn't have lights tonight in the treehouse. The last bits of insulation are in the corner by the door, where the electrical is fixed to plywood boards, the AC already on the wall but with the inverter not working, the DC getting wired up this evening, which is why I almost had to rely on candles. It was getting dark, and I was trying to hook the cable from the battery, now running through holes in the 2x4s of the wall, up through a shelf, and out through the plywood, into a main 80 Amp fuse with a disconnect switch. The little "o" connector barely didn't fit on the bolt of the fuse. What I needed were those "u" shaped ones. There were some in the machine shed, but I didn't have time. They weren't in the cloth bag with all the fiddly electrical bits, or the Star Wars C3PO toy box I use for tools. I'd seen some on the floor, somewhere, but it was getting dark.

I like working with my hands. I'm surprised by the dexterity needed for things like wiring, or installing batts of insulation. There were moments of the paper fronting of the fiberglass tearing free from staples while I was trying to take the weight off with my head, on the top rung of a ladder, where difficulty had me shouting curses as loud as I could into the respirator. Similarly, trying to get a wire to tighten into tiny washers and nuts after dozens of failed attempts had me questioning my life decisions. I decided to skip the disconnect switch and bus bars, splicing the main cable into what was probably too small AWG wire, so it could directly reach the little fuse box I was using before, where I just pull the 20 amp fuses out in lieu of switches.

Beans came by, but when I was too busy to give her food, left again.

Sparks. The lights came on, red and orange. I make bean and cheese quesadillas, using the pot for a plate. Watch an old Popeye Cartoon I downloaded from archive.org.

In the continuity drift novel set farthest in the "past", telepaths take up residences in the boles of trees, which act like psychic stages or amplifiers, broadcasting their thoughts like low-range radios. You can't cut any of the branches, but may use those that fall to make, among other things, large drums. The larger the tree, the deeper the sound.

This seems too portentous, or pretentious, not having written for a while. There is more to explain, threads leading out like strips of glitchy LEDs, context and qualifications.

The stock market crashed, then came back up. In a couple days there may be a plume of toxic lead. I need to take a shower, to wash off the scratch of insulation.

I'm living here, but somehow above the village.

Not only will I have to live with my decisions about the walls, I will have to live in them.

Anyone that ends up as a character in a post or story will be one of those that I send it too. No one will be put online without consent. No doxxing.

All of my friends, it seems (myself included) are designing some kind of a game. J has Stargate. N's is a narrative game that tries to capture improvisational storytelling. B's is called Golemic, and you connect runes on a board, making circuits.

You get points when you complete a circuit. "Like how electricity works," I said.

An example of why I can only write in a literary, not a technical or essayistic mode. I want to connect that little game mechanic with the electric work on Treehouse, the fuses and lights.
